title: Advanced verb patterns
tagline: The verb after the verb changes the meaning: seeing someone leave is not the same as seeing them leaving.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (SAW, SEEM, APPEARS, FORWARD, USED, HELP)
Reading & Use of English Part 3 — word formation with derived verb patterns
Writing Part 2 — precise, varied sentence structure
Speaking Parts 2 and 4 — describing what you witnessed or what you're used to
why: Which form follows a verb — bare infinitive, -ing or to-infinitive — changes the meaning, not just the style: I saw him leave reports a different fact from I saw him leaving. C1 Advanced tests these patterns precisely, especially perception verbs, perfect and continuous infinitives, and fixed expressions like can't help and look forward to.

formula.chip: be/get used to / look forward to

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: I saw him leave before the end of the talk.
I saw him leaving as I arrived.
The teacher made them redo the whole exercise.
She advised him to revise the introduction.
The results seem to have been lost.
He appears to be struggling with the last question.
I can't help wondering if we made the right choice.
be used to / look forward to + -ing
She's used to getting up at five.

use.point: Perception verbs: object + bare infinitive vs. -ing

examples.text: I saw her hand in the assignment just before the bell rang.
I saw her handing in the assignment as I walked past the office.
Nobody heard him say a word all lesson.
examples.note: bare infinitive, a single complete event

examples.text: The manuscript seems to have been written in the early twentieth century.
She appears to have finished the project ahead of schedule.
He seems to be avoiding the question on purpose.
The proposal is expected to be approved by the board next week.
Nobody wants to be left out of the group project.
He apologised for arriving late to the rehearsal.

use.point: can't help/bear/stand and to vs. to + -ing

examples.text: I can't help wondering whether we made the right choice.
She's really looking forward to starting her exchange programme.
examples.note: look forward to + -ing, not bare infinitive

examples.text: After two years abroad, he's finally used to eating spicy food every day.
examples.note: be used to + -ing, contrast with used to + infinitive

watch_out.wrong: I saw him to leave the room.
watch_out.why: Perception verbs (see/hear/watch) take object + bare infinitive, not a to-infinitive.

watch_out.right: The results seem to have been lost.
watch_out.why: An earlier, completed action needs the perfect infinitive: to have been + participle.

watch_out.wrong: He appears struggling with the question.
watch_out.right: He appears to be struggling with the question.
watch_out.why: An ongoing action needs the continuous infinitive: to be + -ing.

watch_out.wrong: She's looking forward to start the exchange programme.
watch_out.right: She's looking forward to starting the exchange programme.
watch_out.why: In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it takes -ing, not the bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: I used to living in Cusco, so the altitude doesn't bother me.
watch_out.right: I am used to living in Cusco, so the altitude doesn't bother me.
watch_out.why: Be/get used to + -ing means 'accustomed to'; used to + infinitive describes a past habit that has stopped.

watch_out.wrong: I can't help to laugh whenever he tells that story.
watch_out.right: I can't help laughing whenever he tells that story.
watch_out.why: Can't help/bear/stand are followed by -ing, not a to-infinitive.

dialogue.title: What exactly did you see?
dialogue.context: Liam and Sofia compare what they noticed backstage during the talent show, while Miss Vega tries to piece the story together.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: So the microphone cut out halfway through Act 3. What did either of you actually see?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I saw Mateo trip over the cable right before it happened.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I didn't see that, but I saw him fixing something backstage just after.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Interesting. Did anyone notice the sound technician?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I heard her say something about a loose connection, but I couldn't hear the rest.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: The cable seems to have been damaged already, honestly, not just unplugged.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: And Mateo — how's he feeling about it now?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: He can't help apologising, even though it clearly wasn't his fault.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I told him I can't help laughing a little, but only because he handled it so calmly.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Well, he's certainly used to dealing with pressure after three years on stage crew.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: True. He's already looking forward to fixing the whole system before the next show.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good attitude. Nobody wants to be blamed for something out of their control.

items.sentence: I ___ leave the room just before the alarm went off.
items.why: Perception verbs take object + bare infinitive for a completed action seen from start to finish.

items.sentence: I ___ as I walked past the classroom.
items.why: -ing shows an action in progress or interrupted, not a completed one.

items.sentence: The manuscript ___ written in the early twentieth century.
items.why: An earlier, completed action needs the perfect infinitive: to have been + participle.

items.sentence: He ___ struggling with the last question.
items.why: An ongoing action needs the continuous infinitive: to be + -ing.

items.sentence: She's really ___ starting her exchange programme.
items.why: In look forward to + -ing, to functions as a preposition.

items.sentence: After two years abroad, he's finally ___ spicy food every day.
items.why: Be/get used to + -ing means accustomed to, unlike used to + infinitive for past habits.

items.sentence: I ___ laughing whenever he tells that story.
items.why: Can't help/bear/stand are followed directly by -ing.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: I saw him ___ (leave) the room just before the bell rang.
I saw him ___ (leave) as I was walking in.
The manuscript seems ___ (write) in the early twentieth century.
He appears ___ (struggle) with the last question.
She's looking forward to ___ (start) her exchange programme.
He's finally used to ___ (eat) spicy food every day.
I can't help ___ (laugh) whenever he tells that story.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: I watched him leave the building before the talk ended.
items.second_end: the building before the talk ended.

items.first: As I arrived, I noticed he was in the middle of leaving.
It's likely that the results were lost somewhere in the system.
It looks like he's struggling with the last question.
She's very excited about starting her exchange programme.
Spicy food doesn't bother him any more after two years abroad.
He always makes me laugh whenever he tells that story, and I just can't stop it.

summary: Perception verbs (see/hear/watch) + object + bare infinitive report a whole action; + -ing reports it in progress.
Perfect infinitives (to have been) point to an earlier action; continuous infinitives (to be -ing) point to one in progress.
Passive infinitives (to be told) and verb + preposition + -ing (apologise for being) follow their own fixed patterns.
can't help/bear/stand + -ing express a reaction you can't control.
look forward to and be/get used to end in the preposition to, so they take -ing, not the bare infinitive.
